'''Ignacio "Nacho" Tinoco Jr.''' (November 22, 1930 – November 15, 2016) was a Professor of [[Chemistry]] at the [[University of California, Berkeley]] from 1956 to 2016.<ref name="Guggenheim">{{cite web |title=Ignacio Tinoco Jr. |url=https://www.gf.org/fellows/all-fellows/ignacio-tinoco-jr/ |website=John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation |accessdate=26 November 2018}}</ref><ref name="Wang">{{cite news |last1=Wang |first1=Linda |title=Ignacio Tinoco dies at age 85 |url=https://cen.acs.org/articles/94/web/2016/11/Ignacio-Tinoco-dies-age-85.html |accessdate=26 November 2018 |work=Chemical & Engineering News |date=2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://chem.berkeley.edu/faculty/emeriti/tinoco/index.php|title=Emeriti Faculty|publisher=[[University of California, Berkeley]]|accessdate=20 February 2013|archive-date=June 20, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120620214843/http://chem.berkeley.edu/faculty/emeriti/tinoco/index.php|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Ignacio Tinoco received a bachelor's degree from the [[University of New Mexico]] in 1951, and a Ph.D. in [[physical chemistry]] at the [[University of Wisconsin, Madison]] in 1954.<ref name="Tinoco2002">{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1146/annurev.physchem.53.082001.144341| pmid = 11972000| title = Physical Chemistry of Nucleic Acids| journal = Annual Review of Physical Chemistry| volume = 53| pages = 1–15| year = 2002| last1 = Tinoco | first1 = I. | bibcode = 2002ARPC...53....1T| doi-access = free}}</ref> He was a postdoctoral fellow with [[John Gamble Kirkwood|John G. Kirkwood]] at [[Yale University]] from 1954 to 1956.<ref name="Tinoco2002"/> He joined the University of California, Berkeley as a faculty member in 1956, where he was professor in the graduate school and a faculty senior scientist, physical biosciences division, [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]]. He was chairman of the chemistry department (1979–82).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://chemistry.berkeley.edu/faculty/chem/tinoco|title=Ignacio Tinoco {{!}} College of Chemistry|website=chemistry.berkeley.edu|language=en|access-date=2018-03-13|archive-date=2018-03-14|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180314042536/https://chemistry.berkeley.edu/faculty/chem/tinoco|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Tinoco, together with [[Carlos Bustamante (biophysicist)]] and Marcos F. Maestre, developed the theory of '''circular intensity differential scattering''' (CIDS),<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Le Gratiet |first1=Aymeric |last2=Marongiu |first2=Riccardo |last3=Diaspro |first3=Alberto |title=Circular Intensity Differential Scattering for Label-Free Chromatin Characterization: A Review for Optical Microscopy |journal=Polymers |year=2020 |volume=12 |issue=10 |page=2428 |doi=10.3390/polym12102428 |doi-access=free |pmid=33096877 |pmc=7588990 }}</ref> showing that the angular differential scattering of left- and right-circularly polarized light can provide information about the geometry and handedness of helical structures.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bustamante |first1=Carlos |last2=Maestre |first2=Marcos F. |last3=Tinoco |first3=Ignacio Jr. |title=Circular intensity differential scattering of light by helical structures. I. Theory |journal=The Journal of Chemical Physics |volume=73 |pages=4273–4281 |year=1980 |issue=9 |doi=10.1063/1.440709 |bibcode=1980JChPh..73.4273B |osti=1133673 }}</ref> In 1982, Tinoco and collaborators experimentally demonstrated angular CIDS from the helical sperm head of the octopus ''Eledone cirrhosa'', observing preferential scattering of one circular polarization with a maximum differential signal of about 2% at a scattering angle of 35°.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Maestre |first1=Marcos F. |last2=Bustamante |first2=Carlos |last3=Hayes |first3=Thomas L. |last4=Subirana |first4=Juan A. |last5=Tinoco |first5=Ignacio Jr. |title=Differential scattering of circularly polarized light by the helical sperm head from the octopus Eledone cirrhosa |journal=Nature |volume=298 |pages=773–774 |year=1982 |issue=5876 |doi=10.1038/298773a0 |pmid=7110315 |bibcode=1982Natur.298..773M }}</ref>

He is known for his pioneering work on [[History of RNA biology#RNA molecules require a specific, complex three-dimensional structure for activity|RNA folding]] and the secondary structures of [[ribonucleic acid]].<ref name="Grens"/><ref name="UHLENBECK">{{cite journal |last1=TINOCO |first1=IGNACIO |last2=UHLENBECK |first2=OLKE C. |last3=LEVINE |first3=MARK D. |title=Estimation of Secondary Structure in Ribonucleic Acids |journal=Nature |date=9 April 1971 |volume=230 |issue=5293 |pages=362–367 |doi=10.1038/230362a0 |pmid=4927725 |bibcode=1971Natur.230..362T |s2cid=4283534 }}</ref><ref name="BORER">{{cite journal |last1=TINOCO |first1=IGNACIO |last2=BORER |first2=PHILIP N. |last3=DENGLER |first3=BARBARA |last4=LEVINE |first4=MARK D. |last5=UHLENBECK |first5=OLKE C. |last6=CROTHERS |first6=DONALD M. |last7=GRALLA |first7=JAY |title=Improved Estimation of Secondary Structure in Ribonucleic Acids |journal=Nature New Biology |date=November 1973 |volume=246 |issue=150 |pages=40–41 |doi=10.1038/newbio246040a0 |pmid=4519026 |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/newbio246040a0 |accessdate=26 November 2018|url-access=subscription }}</ref> His graduate and postdoctoral students include [[Carlos Bustamante (biophysicist)|Carlos Bustamante]] and [[Frances Arnold]].<ref name="Grens">{{cite news |last1=Grens |first1=Kerry |title=Ignacio Tinoco, Luminary of RNA Folding, Dies |url=https://www.the-scientist.com/the-nutshell/ignacio-tinoco-luminary-of-rna-folding-dies-32332 |accessdate=26 November 2018 |work=The Scientist |date=December 20, 2016}}</ref>

His honors and awards include: [[Guggenheim Fellow]], [[Medical Research Council (UK)|Medical Research Council]] Laboratory, Cambridge (1964); California Section Award, [[American Chemical Society]] (1965); D.Sc. University of New Mexico (1972); Member, [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]] (1985); Elisabeth R. Cole Award (Founders Award), [[Biophysical Society]] (1996);<ref>[http://www.biophysics.org/AwardsOpportunities/SocietyAwards/FoundersAward/tabid/502/Default.aspx Founders Award page]</ref> Berkeley Citation, University of California (1996); Member, [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] (2001); [[Emily M. Gray Award]], Biophysical Society (2006); Fellow: [[American Physical Society]], [[Biophysical Society]].

He died on November 15, 2016, at the age of 85.<ref name="Wang"/>

The [[Biophysical Society]] gives the Ignacio Tinoco Award in his honor.<ref name="Biophysical">{{cite web |title=Harry Noller to Receive 2019 BPS Ignacio Tinoco Award |url=https://www.biophysics.org/news-room/harry-noller-to-receive-2019-bps-ignacio-tinoco-award |website=BPS Newsroom |publisher=Biophysical Society |accessdate=26 November 2018}}</ref>
